name: Cognitive Dissonance
statement: Holding clashing beliefs feels uncomfortable, so we change one to ease the tension.
statementAccent: we change one to ease the tension
meaning: Holding two or more contradictory beliefs, or acting against one's own beliefs, produces psychological discomfort that people are motivated to reduce: often by changing an attitude or belief. When what you do conflicts with what you think, the tension pushes you to adjust something so the pieces fit together again.
mechanism: Dissonance is an aversive drive state, unpleasant tension that people act to relieve much as they act to relieve hunger. Its strength grows with the number and importance of the clashing thoughts. People reduce it by changing one of the cognitions, by adding new consonant justifications, by trivialising the conflict, or by avoiding information that would deepen it. A key case is insufficient justification: when the external reason for a counter-attitudinal act is small, people cannot explain the act away, so they change their attitude instead.

examples.text: Students paid a single dollar to tell someone a dull task was fun later rated it more enjoyable than those paid twenty: with little external reason to justify the lie, they changed their attitude to fit their behaviour.
People who undergo a severe initiation to join a group value the group more highly than those admitted easily, justifying the effort by inflating the reward.

When a doomsday group's predicted apocalypse did not arrive, the most committed members did not abandon their belief but intensified it and proselytised: rationalising the disconfirmation rather than accepting it.

variants.name: Effort justification
variants.text: The tendency to value more highly a goal that cost great effort, resolving the dissonance between the effort spent and a disappointing reward.

variants.name: Self-perception theory
variants.text: Bem's competing account, which explains the same results without an aversive drive: people infer their attitudes by observing their own behaviour, as an outside observer would.

whyItMatters: It is one of the most influential theories in social psychology, explaining attitude change, self-justification, rationalisation, and the resilience of belief in the face of contrary evidence. It reframed persuasion and decision-making around the drive for internal consistency, and it remains a lens for understanding everything from consumer choice to political conviction.

working.text: when someone acts against their stated values with little outside reason, expect their attitude to shift to match the act.
to produce lasting attitude change, arrange for behaviour with minimal external inducement, so people internalise the reason.
anticipate that strongly committed people may double down rather than update when evidence contradicts them.

limits: The phenomenon rests on decades of controlled experiments and is among the most cited in the field, but its underlying mechanism is debated. Bem's self-perception theory explains many of the same results without positing an aversive drive, and later work suggests the two accounts may each apply in different ranges. Specific classic paradigms have faced methodological critique, the free-choice paradigm was argued to contain a statistical artefact, and the archival narrative of the doomsday-cult study has been questioned. The core effect is solid; the exact explanation is contested.
misreadings: It is not simply that people are hypocritical: the discomfort of inconsistency is a real motivational state that reshapes attitudes. And the drive account is not the only explanation; self-perception theory reads the same behaviour as people inferring their attitudes from their actions, without any inner tension.
origin: Proposed by Leon Festinger in A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance (1957), with the classic one-dollar experiment reported by Festinger and Carlsmith in 1959 and the doomsday-cult study in When Prophecy Fails (1956).

sources.text: Cognitive dissonance, Wikipedia. — the theory, the one-dollar and effort-justification studies, and Bem's self-perception alternative.
Festinger & Carlsmith, "Cognitive Consequences of Forced Compliance," Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 58:203-210 (1959).
